## The one-line version

`schedule:inventory` reports the timers of **whichever process answers the call**. That is
normally the operator (`:3070`). Most recurring sweeps do not run there — they run in
`papercup-bg-host.service`. So for those, the inventory has always answered *"not here"*,
and *"not here"* reads exactly like *"does not exist"*.

## What it cost

`dbos-executor-reaper` failed on **every single pass for 6+ days** on a float-to-bigint
bind. `attention-reconcile-unanswerable` had **never executed once** — and when it finally
ran it resolved 195 stale escalations, dropping the past-48h backlog 315 → 120 in one
sweep. Neither was visible from `schedule:inventory`.

The detector for "an armed timer is erroring" already existed and already carried
`armed` + `lastFire` + `lastError`. It was simply **pointed at the wrong process**. The
defect was ROUTING, not a missing mechanism — which is why the fix federates the existing
registry rather than inventing a heartbeat. (An earlier draft of the fix *was* a new
heartbeat; the claim-time premise guard caught the underlying "there is no such surface"
claim as an unverified absence, and the surface turned out to be one file away.)

## There are TWO per-process registries, and the second one is the one that matters

This is the part that is easy to get wrong, and it nearly shipped wrong.

| slice | mechanism | where the state lives |
|---|---|---|
| `source: 'managed'` | `managedSetInterval` | in-memory registry of the serving process |
| `source: 'dbos'` | DBOS scheduled workflows | **also** in-memory — the SDK registry, populated when the workflow modules are *imported* |

`dbos-schedule-introspect.ts` says it plainly: DBOS keeps schedule definitions *"only in an
in-process registry populated when the workflow modules are imported."* The modules behind
`PAPERCUSP_BACKGROUND_WORKERS` are imported **only in bg-host** — and both sweeps above are
DBOS periodic workflows (`dbos/periodic-workflows.ts`), not `managedSetInterval` timers.

So a federation that carried only the managed timers would have been green, typechecked,
live-verified — and would have **missed the outage that motivated it**. If you are extending
this, check the *named* failing thing appears, not merely that the mechanism works.

Fire-state is the exception that makes this tractable: `lastFireMs`/`lastStatus` come from
shared Postgres (`dbos.event_dispatch_kv`), so only the *names and crontabs* are stranded
per-process. A sibling hands over its registry; the operator enriches it centrally.

## How to read the inventory now

Sibling operator-shaped processes — anything serving `bin/hono-host.ts` (bg-host, staging) —
are federated over a bounded loopback probe:

- **`detail.federated: true`** — a LIVE row from another process. `detail.process` names it
  (`bg-host:3271`). `armed`/`lastFire`/`lastError` are real.
- **`detail.federated: false`** — either the static `EXTERNAL_PROCESS_TIMERS` manifest (the
  inference gateway, its watchdog, psu-launcher — they serve no such endpoint), or a sibling
  that **did not answer**, rendered as one explicit `… (timers unknown)` row.
- **Unknown is not absent.** The degraded row exists precisely so that silence is visible.
  Dropping it would restore the original bug.

⚠ The two slices land under **different sources on purpose**:

- sibling **managed** timers → `source: 'external-process'` (ephemeral tier), so they enter
  `poll-suspect-alarm`'s timer-registration audit, which consumes exactly
  `in-process | managed | external-process`.
- sibling **DBOS** schedules → `source: 'dbos'`, `tier: 'durable'`. Two reasons: an operator
  auditing `source: 'dbos'` is the audience that missed the reaper, and that same
  poll-suspect audit deliberately EXCLUDES the durable tier (WI-6094) — tagging them
  `external-process` would drag them into an audit explicitly scoped to exclude them.

Where a federated row goes is a **consumer** question, not a taxonomy one. Ask who filters
on the source, not what the row "is".

Federated DBOS rows dedupe against local ones by name: a schedule registered in both
processes is ONE logical schedule (DBOS coordinates it through shared Postgres, so both
copies carry identical fire-state). Federation adds what was missing; it never
double-reports.

## Mechanism

- **`GET /api/internal/managed-timers`** (`auth: 'loopback'`) — each process reports its own
  two registries. Deliberately a **pure in-memory read**: it does NOT call
  `collectScheduleInventory`, which queries Postgres and DBOS and is the call measured
  returning **zero bytes for 45s** against `:3271`. The process least able to afford I/O is
  exactly the one you most need to ask, so the probe must be cheaper than its target.
- **`schedule-federation.ts`** — discovery + the bounded probe.

### Discovery reuses a registry that already existed

Every operator-shaped process already publishes `~/.papercusp/endpoint-ipc.<port>.json`
(`socketPath`, `pid`, `startedAt`, `port`) on boot and prunes siblings whose pid is dead.
That is a live process registry, so there is **no hard-coded unit→port map** to rot.

Two traps if you touch this:

- `ownHonoPort()` must stay expression-identical to the discovery-file **writer**
  (`Number(PAPERCUSP_HONO_PORT) || 3070`). If they diverge, a process stops recognising its
  own advertisement and **federates itself**, double-counting every one of its timers. A test
  pins this.
- Only the **per-port** files are read. The legacy singleton `endpoint-ipc.json` is
  last-writer-wins across every operator on the box, so including it would duplicate a
  sibling or point at a different process than its filename implies.

### A wedged sibling must not become a wedged operator

bg-host has been measured accepting a connection and then returning nothing for 45s while
staying alive and working (its `/api/health` went dark and recovered). A fan-out that waits
on that trades a visibility bug for an availability bug. So:

- per-probe `AbortSignal.timeout` — which aborts the **body read**, not just the connect;
  the observed failure mode is a connection that opens and then stalls, which a connect-only
  timeout sails straight past;
- a hard budget race **per probe, not per fan-out** — so one wedged sibling degrades alone
  and healthy siblings still report. A whole-set race would discard good data to punish one
  bad process;
- `probeSibling` **never rejects** — every failure becomes an `ok: false` row.

The recurrence guard is a test whose fetch stub is deliberately *worse than reality*: it
ignores its `AbortSignal` entirely, so only the outer budget can save the call.

## Worse than per-process: it was per-MODULE-INSTANCE (2026-08-03, EI-19451658870832332)

Federating across processes was necessary and it was **not sufficient**. Asking the *right*
process still returned a wrong answer, because one process held **two registries**.

`dbos-executor-reaper` was reaping workflows every 2 minutes inside `papercup-bg-host` —
visible the whole time in `journalctl --user -u papercup-bg-host` as
`[dbos-executor-reaper] reaped 1 workflow(s) …` — while absent from
`/api/internal/managed-timers` **served by that same pid**. Both readings were correct:

- `managedSetInterval` registers unconditionally, and `listManaged()` filters nothing
  (`libs/generic/scheduled-registry/src/index.ts`). A single instance cannot produce both.
- So there were **two live instances of `@papercusp/scheduled-registry` in one process**,
  each with its own module-level `const registry = new Map()`.

The host entry runs under tsx (a CJS preflight alongside an ESM loader), importers reach the
package through both bare-specifier and relative paths, and `node_modules/@papercusp/*` are
symlinks into the repo. Any one of those seams yields two module records.

**The fix does not depend on knowing which seam did it.** The registry's mutable state is now
pinned to `globalThis` under a `Symbol.for(...)` key — correct under dual-package, symlink,
CJS/ESM-split and bundled-copy alike. `configureScheduledRegistry`'s seams are shared too, so
a hidden instance can no longer quietly run with default seams (i.e. ignoring the host's
tick-load-shed).

### Two traps this burned, both worth internalising

**A negative result only covers the conditions it actually reproduced.** A controlled tsx
probe "FALSIFIED" the dual-instance hypothesis — importing the registry statically and the
reaper by package subpath, with a control proving the import path was exercised. It was a
sound experiment that did not recreate the host's real loader conditions, and it sent the
investigation to a dead end for a full wake. A probe's `false` is scoped to its setup.

**Unobservable is not empty.** `:3070` has no `/api/internal/managed-timers` route at all —
it returns `{"error":"not_found"}`, because the route does not exist in the release build. A
`json.get('timers', [])` parse renders that as `total 0`, i.e. a *false zero* shaped exactly
like a measurement. Any process eliminated "by measurement" through that endpoint was never
actually measured.

**Guard:** `libs/generic/scheduled-registry/src/index.test.ts` re-evaluates the module via
`vi.resetModules()` and asserts the two instances share one inventory. It ships with a
**calibration control** (`module-scoped-control.fixture.ts`) that asserts module-scoped state
does *not* survive the same reset — because if `resetModules()` ever stopped producing a
second instance, the guard would pass vacuously and the hazard would walk right back in.

## The generalisable lesson

**Per-process in-memory state read through a single-process surface produces a confident,
well-formed, wrong answer** — and the wrong answer is an *absence*, which is the shape
agents are least equipped to doubt. Before concluding "X is not registered / not running /
does not exist", ask **which process you just asked** — and, per the section above, whether
that process holds more than one copy of the thing you are asking about. Related: an
inventory that answers only about itself should say so in its own output; this one now does,
via `detail.process`.

The sharper form, learned the expensive way: **an inventory's absence is evidence only if
there is exactly ONE inventory.** Establish that before spending a wake on what the absence
"means".
